name: Clinical Neuro-Localization Rules and UMN vs LMN Distinctions

reference.source: Clinical Neuroanatomy Made Ridiculously Simple / Brazis Localization
clinicalPearls: UMN lesions produce spasticity, clasp-knife tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, and positive extensor Babinski sign
LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, denervation atrophy, and visible fasciculations
Brainstem rule of 4: 4 cranial nerves in medulla (IX-XII), 4 in pons (V-VIII), 4 above/midbrain (I-IV)
Medial brainstem structures: motor pathway (corticospinal), medial lemniscus, MLF, and motor cranial nerve nuclei
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: PICA occlusion causing dysphagia, hoarseness, Horner, and crossed analgesia
reference.pathophysiology: Accurate neurological diagnosis relies on anatomic localization derived from neurological signs. Motor weakness is categorized into central upper motor neuron dysfunction (loss of cortical inhibitory tone) versus peripheral lower motor neuron dysfunction (denervation of motor units). Brainstem vascular lesions combine ipsilateral cranial nerve signs with contralateral body deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (combined UMN and LMN signs)
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (EMG/NCS) for LMN denervation versus myopathy
MRI brain and spinal cord with gadolinium
Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis for inflammatory neuro-immunology
